title: Weight regain and cardiometabolic effects after withdrawal of semaglutide: The STEP 1 trial extension
authors: Wilding, Batterham, Davies, Van Gaal, Kandler, Konakli, Lingvay, McGowan, Oral, Rosenstock, Wadden, Wharton, Yokote, Zeuthen and Kushner
topic: what happens after stopping GLP-1 weight loss medication
researchQuestion: What happens to weight and cardiometabolic markers after semaglutide is stopped?
changedOrCompared: Participants who had been using semaglutide during the trial were followed after treatment withdrawal.
measured: Body weight and cardiometabolic markers after stopping treatment.
finding: One year after stopping semaglutide, participants regained about two thirds of their prior weight loss.
doesNotProve: It does not prove GLP-1 medications are bad or useless. It shows that stopping treatment without ongoing support can lead to regain.
humanTakeaway: Medication can lower the difficulty, but the long-term plan still matters.
slideTitle: GLP-1s work. The exit plan matters.

title: Mind-set matters: Exercise and the placebo effect
topic: how belief can affect health markers
researchQuestion: Can changing how people think about their daily movement affect health markers?
changedOrCompared: Hotel cleaners were told that their work counted as exercise and met physical activity guidelines.
measured: Weight, blood pressure, body fat, waist-to-hip ratio, perceived exercise and reported exercise outside work.
finding: After four weeks, the informed group showed improvements in several health markers without reporting more exercise outside work.
doesNotProve: It does not prove belief replaces movement or breaks physics. The cleaners were already doing physical work.
humanTakeaway: How you frame movement can affect how you value it, notice it, and possibly how your body responds.

title: Mind over milkshakes: Mindsets, not just nutrients, determine ghrelin response
topic: how belief about food can affect hunger signals
researchQuestion: Can beliefs about the same food change the body's hunger-hormone response?
changedOrCompared: Participants drank the same milkshake on different visits, but saw labels that framed it as indulgent or sensible.
measured: Ghrelin response. Ghrelin is one of the hormones tied to hunger.
finding: When participants believed the shake was indulgent, ghrelin dropped more than when they believed it was sensible.
doesNotProve: It does not prove people can think calories away or ignore nutrition. The shake was still the same food.
humanTakeaway: What someone believes about a meal can influence how their body responds to it.

title: High-Protein Plant-Based Diet Versus a Protein-Matched Omnivorous Diet to Support Resistance Training Adaptations
authors: Hevia-Larrain, Gualano, Longobardi, Gil, Fernandes, Costa, Pereira, Artioli, Phillips and Roschel
researchQuestion: Can a high-protein plant-based diet support resistance-training gains similarly to a protein-matched omnivorous diet?
changedOrCompared: A plant-based diet using soy protein was compared with an omnivorous diet using whey and animal foods while both groups trained.
measured: Muscle mass and strength after twelve weeks of resistance training.
finding: Both groups gained muscle and strength, with no meaningful difference between groups when protein and training were handled.
doesNotProve: It does not prove every protein food is identical. It shows plant-based diets can work when total protein and training are set up properly.
humanTakeaway: Plant-based muscle gain is not about magic foods. It is about enough protein, good training, and consistency.

title: Effects of Resistance Training Frequency on Measures of Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
topic: how often to train for muscle growth
researchQuestion: How much does weekly training frequency matter for muscle growth?
changedOrCompared: The review compared different resistance-training frequencies across studies.
finding: Training frequency can matter, but much of the practical result depends on total weekly training volume.
doesNotProve: It does not prove one split is universally best. It suggests the split is a tool for distributing enough quality work.
humanTakeaway: Pick a split you can repeat, then make sure the weekly work is hard enough and recoverable.
slideTitle: Three days or six? Volume decides.
kicker: Split is a tool, not magic

title: Ultra-Processed Diets Cause Excess Calorie Intake and Weight Gain: An Inpatient Randomized Controlled Trial of Ad Libitum Food Intake
authors: Hall, Ayuketah, Brychta, Cai, Cassimatis, Chen, Chung, Costa, Courville, Darcey, Fletcher, Forde, Gharib, Guo, Howard, Joseph, McGehee, Ouwerkerk, Raisinger, Rozga, Stagliano, Walter, Walter, Yang and Zhou
topic: why ultra-processed food can make overeating easier
researchQuestion: What happens to calorie intake and body weight when people eat ultra-processed foods compared with unprocessed foods in a controlled setting?
changedOrCompared: Twenty adults lived in an inpatient research unit. Each participant ate both diets in a randomized order: two weeks of ultra-processed meals and two weeks of unprocessed meals. The diets were matched for presented calories, sugar, fat, fibre, sodium, and macronutrients, and people could eat as much or as little as they wanted.
measured: Daily calorie intake and body weight.
finding: People ate about five hundred more calories per day on the ultra-processed diet and gained weight, while they lost weight on the unprocessed diet.
doesNotProve: It doesn't prove every packaged food is automatically bad or that one meal ruins anything. It shows that the food environment and level of processing can make overeating easier without people trying to overeat.
humanTakeaway: Ultra-processed food can make overeating easier, even when meals look matched.

title: Insufficient sleep undermines dietary efforts to reduce adiposity
authors: Nedeltcheva, Kilkus, Imperial, Schoeller and Penev
topic: why sleep can change weight loss quality
researchQuestion: Does sleep restriction change how much of diet-induced weight loss comes from fat versus fat-free mass?
changedOrCompared: Ten overweight adults lived in a clinical research centre during two fourteen-day calorie-restricted diet periods. Each participant completed both sleep conditions in random order: eight and a half hours of sleep opportunity and five and a half hours of sleep opportunity.
measured: Total weight loss, fat loss, fat-free mass loss, hunger, energy expenditure, and metabolic hormones.
finding: Total weight loss was similar, but sleep restriction reduced the proportion of weight lost as fat by 55 percent and increased the loss of fat-free mass by 60 percent.
doesNotProve: It does not prove one bad night ruins fat loss or that sleep replaces nutrition. It shows sleep can affect the quality of weight loss during a calorie deficit.
humanTakeaway: If you're dieting, sleep matters for what you lose, not just how much.

title: Breaking Up Prolonged Sitting Reduces Postprandial Glucose and Insulin Responses
authors: Dunstan, Kingwell, Larsen, Healy, Cerin, Hamilton, Shaw, Bertovic, Zimmet, Salmon and Owen
topic: how short walking breaks can change blood sugar after meals
researchQuestion: Can breaking up prolonged sitting with short walking breaks reduce post-meal glucose and insulin responses?
changedOrCompared: Nineteen overweight or obese adults completed three lab visits in randomized order: uninterrupted sitting, sitting interrupted with two-minute light walking breaks every twenty minutes, and sitting interrupted with two-minute moderate walking breaks every twenty minutes.
measured: Blood sugar and insulin responses for five hours after a standardized test drink.
finding: Compared with uninterrupted sitting, both walking-break conditions lowered the post-meal blood sugar and insulin response.
doesNotProve: It does not prove walking breaks replace exercise, nutrition, or medical care. It shows that breaking up long sitting can acutely change the body's response after meals.
humanTakeaway: If you're sitting for hours, break it up with short walks.

title: Exercise training increases size of hippocampus and improves memory
authors: Erickson, Voss, Prakash, Basak, Szabo, Chaddock, Kim, Heo, Alves, White, Wojcicki, Mailey, Vieira, Martin, Pence, Woods, McAuley and Kramer
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
topic: whether aerobic exercise can change the brain
researchQuestion: Can aerobic exercise training increase hippocampal volume and improve memory in older adults?
changedOrCompared: One hundred and twenty older adults were randomized to one year of aerobic walking exercise or a stretching and toning control program.
measured: Hippocampus volume measured with brain imaging, spatial memory, fitness, and blood markers related to brain plasticity.
finding: The aerobic exercise group increased anterior hippocampus volume by about two percent and improved spatial memory, while the control group showed hippocampus volume decline.
doesNotProve: It does not prove walking cures dementia or that every person gets the same brain change. It shows regular aerobic exercise can change brain structure and memory-related outcomes in older adults.
humanTakeaway: Regular aerobic exercise is not just for fitness. It can support brain health too.

title: The impact of food order on postprandial glycaemic excursions in prediabetes
authors: Shukla, Dickison, Coughlin, Karan, Mauer, Truong, Casper, Emiliano, Kumar, Saunders, Igel and Aronne
topic: whether the order you eat food can change blood sugar
researchQuestion: Can eating the same meal in a different order change post-meal blood sugar and insulin responses in people with prediabetes?
changedOrCompared: Fifteen adults with prediabetes ate the same meal on three separate days in randomized order: carbohydrates first, protein and vegetables first, or vegetables first.
measured: Blood glucose and insulin responses for three hours after the meal.
finding: Eating protein and vegetables before carbohydrates lowered post-meal glucose exposure compared with eating carbohydrates first, and the vegetables-first order produced the lowest insulin response.
doesNotProve: It does not prove food order cures prediabetes or matters equally for every meal. It shows the sequence of the same foods can change the short-term blood sugar response.
humanTakeaway: Protein and vegetables before carbohydrates may smooth the blood sugar response.

title: The impact of food order on postprandial glycaemic excursions in prediabetes
authors: Shukla, Dickison, Coughlin, Karan, Mauer, Truong, Casper, Emiliano, Kumar, Saunders, Igel and Aronne
topic: whether the order you eat food can change blood sugar
researchQuestion: Can eating the same meal in a different order change post-meal blood sugar and insulin responses in people with prediabetes?
changedOrCompared: Fifteen adults with prediabetes ate the same meal on three separate days in randomized order: carbohydrates first, protein and vegetables first, or vegetables first.
measured: Blood glucose and insulin responses for three hours after the meal.
finding: Eating protein and vegetables before carbohydrates lowered post-meal glucose exposure compared with eating carbohydrates first, and the vegetables-first order produced the lowest insulin response.
doesNotProve: It does not prove food order cures prediabetes or matters equally for every meal. It shows the sequence of the same foods can change the short-term blood sugar response.
humanTakeaway: Protein and vegetables before carbohydrates may smooth the blood sugar response a bit.

title: Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
topic: how evening screen reading can affect sleep
researchQuestion: Does reading from a light-emitting device before bed affect sleep, melatonin, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness compared with a printed book?
changedOrCompared: Twelve healthy adults read for four hours before bed for five evenings using a light-emitting e-reader, and for five evenings using a printed book, in randomized order.
measured: Time to fall asleep, melatonin secretion, circadian timing, sleep structure, and next-morning alertness.
finding: Compared with reading a printed book, the light-emitting e-reader made people take longer to fall asleep, suppressed melatonin, shifted the body clock later, and reduced next-morning alertness.
doesNotProve: It does not prove every screen minute ruins sleep or that blue light is the only factor. It shows prolonged bright screen reading before bed can push sleep biology in the wrong direction.
humanTakeaway: If sleep matters tonight, make the last hour dimmer and less screen-heavy.

title: Association of Efficacy of Resistance Exercise Training With Depressive Symptoms: Meta-analysis and Meta-regression Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
authors: Gordon, McDowell, Hallgren, Meyer, Lyons and Herring
topic: whether resistance training can help depressive symptoms
researchQuestion: Across randomized clinical trials, is resistance exercise training associated with lower depressive symptoms in adults?
changedOrCompared: The researchers pooled thirty-three randomized clinical trials comparing resistance exercise training with non-active control conditions.
measured: Depressive symptom scores before and after the interventions.
finding: Resistance exercise training was associated with a moderate reduction in depressive symptoms compared with non-active controls.
doesNotProve: It does not prove lifting replaces therapy, medication, or professional care. It shows resistance training can be a useful support for depressive symptoms.
humanTakeaway: Lifting is not just about muscle. It can be part of a mental-health support plan too.

title: Do stair climbing exercise snacks improve cardiorespiratory fitness?
authors: Jenkins, Nairn, Skelly, Little and Gibala
topic: whether tiny exercise snacks can improve fitness
researchQuestion: Can very brief stair-climbing exercise snacks improve peak oxygen uptake in sedentary young adults?
changedOrCompared: Sedentary young adults were randomly assigned to either a non-training control group or stair-climbing exercise snacks. The exercise group vigorously climbed a three-flight stairwell three times per day, three days per week, for six weeks.
measured: Peak oxygen uptake, a measure of cardiorespiratory fitness.
finding: Peak oxygen uptake was higher in the stair-climbing group after the intervention, suggesting improved cardiorespiratory fitness, although the absolute increase was modest.
doesNotProve: It does not prove a few stair climbs replace a full training plan or that this works the same for every population. It shows small hard bursts can improve fitness in inactive people.
humanTakeaway: If a full workout feels impossible, a few hard stair climbs can still count.
